Missense, nonsense, and microdeletions impact large-scale networks, but the consequences of extensive deletions for long-term disease resilience remain understudied. Many transcriptomes express diverse subpopulations, and transcription level sparsity can differentially modulate network structure. Here we uncover the molecular underpinnings of each of these three modes of disease resilience using yeast as a system. To this end, we perform single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) on the Smt2 T-cell transcriptome from the primary infection stage on through the disease resolution process (DRP) to convalescence. We capture phenotypes in single cells using artificial and natural pathways of natural gradient projection (NHG-PGPR). Together, these experiments reveal that, while significant Smt2 cell depletion (notably suppression) is a common characteristic among Smt2 cells, most of the cells expressing Smt2 genes do not show significant phenotypes. Using the molecular annotations in the human and mouse Smt2 gene clusters, we highlight noncoding RNA (ncrRNA) and small RNA (sRNA) as key contributors to each phenotype, suggesting that transcriptional plasticity within ncrRNA and sRNA is key to restore transcriptomes to near-normal. Our findings reveal distinct phenotypes associated with each of the three major modes of disease resilience and provide an essential, but previously overlooked, insight into the molecular underpinnings of long-term resilience.

Data sharing is critical to supporting research and ensuring reproducibility. However, many bioinformatics tools do not provide data sharing capabilities. This is particularly concerning in biomedicine where researchers are typically under resource constraints. Here, we present DAPFER (Data Acquisition for Planning Efficient and Reusable inference of Single-cell transcriptomes), a new open-source R package for the automated generation of scripts to acquire raw data from secondary sequencing reactions, normalize and prepare cells, and derive robust Sef estimates from single-cell sequencing experiments. This R package contains two main components: DAPFER (2) (dapfer) - a pipeline for generating Sef estimates from both default- and specified Sef parameters - and data transformation to apply the Sef to individual cells, using pipelines allowing for the incorporation of additional parameters, allowing for a flexible consideration of spatial and temporal variation. When combined, these components enable researchers to conduct the first step of data-analysis of single-cell sequencing experiments. These tools enable researchers to create Sef estimates and, in doing so, provide an integrated solution for primary data-analysis.

Data analysis using DAPFER provides automated Sef estimates with few to no user-interactions, thereby drastically reducing research burden and the time to submit results. Data sharing is thus facilitated and made more efficient, improving reproducibility and scientific progress. This package aims to provide a practical and efficient solution for data analysis to achieve Sef for researchers and thus promote research progress.

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is an evolving method for single-cell biological data analysis and is now broadly applied to study cells across diverse organisms. With current progress in scRNA-seq, it is becoming increasingly necessary to analyze the quality of data generated by scRNA-seq, particularly to correlate with published data in high-throughput databases such as Gene Ontology (GO) and Gene Ontology (GO-seq). Here, we build a 1) robust pipeline to account for differences in classification errors between scRNA-seq and standard single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) annotations, and 2) a high-performance, scalable tool to re-produce previously published GO annotations to verify that they accurately describe cell identities. Using the tool, we derive seven quantitative metrics for scRNA-seq classification. Next, we evaluated scRNA-seq classification errors using three examples of classical biological databases: Saccharomyces cerevisiae Dunn et al. (2014) (1) Gene Ontology (2) Model Organisms and (3) Saccharomyces cerevisiae Reference. Two independent sources of data are used as test systems. For each test system, we provide testable thresholds for classification errors, which we identify as false discovery rates (FDRs). We selected F-scores, which reflect the proportion of examples that are misclassified, as the objective measure of accuracy, and simulated classification errors associated with F-score values between 0.01 and 1.01. The simulations demonstrate that, for F-score values between 0.01 and 0.1, correct classifications exceed false-classified examples. With a F-score value between 0.1 and 0.05, we observe an FDR threshold of 0.05, sufficient to distinguish true cell identities from other types of cells. Our work contributes to the development of robust scRNA-seq analyses by providing testing principles for improved classification, while further supporting high-performance analysis.

In the context of single-cell genomics, mapping genomic regions of interest (ROIs) to cells is essential for analyzing cell-specific expression profiles. There are several common and established approaches to mapping genomic regions of interest to cells, including positional cloning, Sanger sequencing, and short-read-based approaches such as synteny mapping. We developed a new pipeline to identify markers for chromosome boundaries in the mammalian somatic cell set, the CC{1} (also called B{3} or C{3} somatic cells), using short reads from a 3D massively parallel cloning (3D-CLONE) array. In order to reduce false positives due to fragmentation between chromosomes, we used custom read error rate (RER) metrics, specifically the probability of a particular read to be mapped within a chromosome. We used these read errors to identify regions around genes of interest, which we refer to as "annotation reads." In this way, we were able to identify markers of chromosomal boundaries without false positives, and with a large volume of read data.

Implications

This pipeline is useful for many fields that require cell-specific genomic annotation, such as epigenetics, germ-line cell lineages, genomic imprinting, and germline mutations. This pipeline is particularly useful for determining the chromosome extent of monogenic diseases where there is a need for localization of markers to a particular chromosome.
sample_p_texts: Single cells exhibit heterogeneous gene expression profiles and chromatin accessibility, measurable separately via single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell transposase chromatin accessibility sequencing (scATAC-seq). Consequently, each cell possesses a unique gene regulatory network. However, limited methods exist for inferring cell-specific regulatory networks, particularly through the integration of scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data. Here, we develop a novel algorithm named single-cell regulatory network inference (ScReNI), which leverages k-nearest neighbors and random forest algorithms to integrate scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data for inferring gene regulatory networks at the single-cell level. ScReNI is built to analyze both paired and unpaired datasets for scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq. Using these two types of single-cell sequencing datasets, we validate that a higher fraction of regulatory relationships inferred by ScReNI are detected by chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) data. ScReNI shows superior performance in network-based cell clustering when compared to existing single-cell network inference methods. Importantly, ScReNI offers the unique function of identifying cell-enriched regulators based on each cell-specific network. In summary, ScReNI facilitates the inferences of cell-specific regulatory networks and cell-enriched regulators.

Chevreul is an open-source R Bioconductor package and interactive R Shiny app for processing and visualization of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. It differs from other scRNA- seq analysis packages in its ease of use, its capacity to analyze full-length RNA sequencing data for exon coverage and transcript isoform inference, and its support for batch correction. Chevreul enables exploratory analysis of scRNA-seq data using Bioconductor SingleCellExperiment or Seurat objects. Simple processing functions with sensible default settings enable batch integration, quality control filtering, read count normalization and transformation, dimensionality reduction, clustering at a range of resolutions, and cluster marker gene identification. Processed data can be visualized in an interactive R Shiny app with dynamically linked plots. Expression of gene or transcript features can be displayed on PCA, tSNE, and UMAP embeddings, heatmaps, or violin plots while differential expression can be evaluated with several statistical tests without extensive programming. Existing analysis tools do not provide specialized tools for isoform-level analysis or alternative splicing detection. By enabling isoform-level expression analysis for differential expression, dimensionality reduction and batch integration, Chevreul empowers researchers without prior programming experience to analyze full-length scRNA-seq data.

Data availabilityA test dataset formatted as a SingleCellExperiment object can be found at https://github.com/cobriniklab/chevreuldata.

Availability & ImplementationChevreul is implemented in R and the R package and integrated Shiny application are freely available at https://github.com/cobriniklab/chevreul.

Single-cell multiomic technologies have allowed unprecedented access to gene profiles of individual cells across species and organ systems, including >1000 papers focused on brain cell types alone. The Allen Institute has created foundational atlases characterizing mammalian brain cell types in the adult mouse brain and the neocortex of aged humans with and without Alzheimers disease (AD). With so many public cell type classifications (or  taxonomies) available and many groups choosing to define their own, linking cell types and associated knowledge between studies remains a major challenge. Here, we introduce Annotation Comparison Explorer (ACE), a web application for comparing cell type assignments and other cell-based annotations (e.g., donor demographics, anatomic locations, batch variables, and quality control metrics). ACE allows filtering of cells and includes an interactive set of tools for comparing two or more taxonomy annotations alongside collected knowledge (e.g., increased abundance in disease conditions, cell type aliases, or other information about a specific cell type). We present three primary use cases for ACE. First, we demonstrate how a user can assign cell type labels from the Seattle Alzheimers Disease Brain Cell Atlas (SEA-AD) taxonomy to cells from their own study and compare these cell type mappings to existing cell type assignments and cell metadata. Second, we extend this approach to ten published human AD studies which we previously reprocessed through a common data analysis pipeline. This allowed us to compare brain taxonomies across otherwise incomparable studies and identify congruent cell type abundance changes in AD, including a decrease in abundance of subsets of somatostatin interneurons. Finally, ACE includes translation tables between different mouse and human brain cell type taxonomies publicly accessible on Allen Brain Map, from initial studies in individual neocortical areas to more recent studies spanning the whole brain. ACE can be freely and publicly accessed as a web application (https://sea-ad.shinyapps.io/ACEapp/) and on GitHub (github.com/AllenInstitute/ACE).

A key challenge in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis is clustering cells based on their expression profiles. Effective clustering requires selecting the most informative gene features whose varying expression levels in different cell types can be used to discriminate between different cell types. This study introduces DIFS, a novel statistical framework designed to enhance discriminative feature selection for scRNA-seq-based cell clustering. DIFS operates in two stages. In the first stage, a modified dip test identifies genes with significant multimodal expression patterns, as these are likely to have different expression levels in different cell types. In the second stage, cells are clustered based on the selected features from stage one, and additional cluster-specific features are identified, capturing genes that may be expressed in only one cell cluster. Through real data analysis, we demonstrate that DIFS improves the accuracy of cell type classification and enhances the understanding of cellular heterogeneity in single-cell studies.

A major challenge in scRNAseq analysis is how to recover the biologically meaningful cell ontology tree and conserved gene modules across datasets. Data integration and batch-effect correction have been the key to effectively analyze multiple datasets, but often fail to disentangle cell states in heterogeneous samples, such as in cancer and the immune system. Here we present super single cell clustering (SuperSCC), a novel algorithm that utilizes machine-learning models to discover cell identities and gene modules from multiple datasets without the need of data integration. Of note, SuperSCC can be implemented both in cell lineage and cell state level, thereby building the hierarchy of cell programs with specific cell identity and gene modules. Such information has the great potential to identify the shared rare populations across datasets regardless of batch effect and benefits label transfer for mapping cell labels from reference to query. We used SuperSCC to perform atlas level data analysis on more than 90 datasets and build a cell state map of complex tissue in healthy and diseased stages, such as human lung. We show that SuperSCC outperforms existing approaches in identifying cellular context, has better annotation accuracy, and outlines gene modules that indicate conserved immune cell status in lung microenvironments.

Leveraging single cell reference atlases to analyse new data has brought about a paradigm shift in single cell data science akin to the first reference genome in genomics. However methods to perform this mapping require computational expertise as well as sometimes considerable compute power, and thus may exclude the researchers from this innovation who may benefit the most from it. ArchMap, a no-code query-to-reference mapping tool, removes this barrier by providing all-in-one automated mapping, cell type annotation, and collaborative features to analyse single-cell datasets from a wide range of integrated, often published, reference atlases and allows extension of atlases with the growing Human Cell Atlas and related efforts. This paves the way for a democratisation of reference mapping capabilities.

The identification of cell types remains a major challenge. Even after a decade of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), reasonable cell type annotations almost always include manual non-automated steps. The identification of orthologous cell types across species complicates matters even more, but at the same time strengthens the confidence in the assignment. Here, we generate and analyze a dataset consisting of embryoid bodies (EBs) derived from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) of four primate species: humans, orangutans, cynomolgus, and rhesus macaques. This kind of data includes a continuum of developmental cell types, multiple batch effects (i.e. species and individuals) and uneven cell type compositions and hence poses many challenges. We developed a semi-automated computational pipeline combining classification and marker based cluster annotation to identify orthologous cell types across primates. This approach enabled the investigation of cross-species conservation of gene expression. Consistent with previous studies, our data confirm that broadly expressed genes are more conserved than cell type-specific genes, raising the question how conserved - inherently cell type-specific - marker genes are. Our analyses reveal that human marker genes are less effective in macaques and vice versa, highlighting the limited transferability of markers across species. Overall, our study advances the identification of orthologous cell types across species, provides a well-curated cell type reference for future in vitro studies and informs the transferability of marker genes across species.

Long-read RNA sequencing has transformed transcriptome analysis by enabling comprehensive mapping of full-length transcripts, providing an unprecedented resolution of transcript diversity, alternative splicing, and transcript-specific regulation. In this study, we employed nanopore long-read RNA sequencing to profile the transcriptomes of human fibroblasts, induced pluripotent stem cells, and stem cell-derived cortical neurons, identifying extensive transcript diversity with 15,072 transcripts in stem cell-derived cortical neurons, 13,048 in fibroblasts, and 12,759 in induced pluripotent stem cells. Our analyses uncovered 35,519 differential transcript expression events and 5,135 differential transcript usage events, underscoring the complexity of transcriptomic regulation across these cell types. Importantly, by integrating differential transcript expression and usage analyses, we gained deeper insights into transcript dynamics that are not captured by gene-level expression analysis alone. Notably, differential transcript usage analysis highlighted transcript-specific changes in disease-relevant genes such as APP, KIF2A, and BSCL2, associated with Alzheimers disease, neuronal migration disorders, and degenerative axonopathies, respectively. This added resolution emphasizes the significance of transcript- level variations that often remain hidden in traditional differential gene expression analyses.

Overall, our work provides a framework for understanding transcript diversity in both pluripotent and specialized cell types, which can be used to investigate transcriptomic changes in disease states. Additionally, this study underscores the utility of differential transcript usage analysis in advancing our understanding of neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases, paving the way for identifying transcript-specific therapeutic targets.

Single-cell RNA sequencing has revolutionized the study of cellular heterogeneity, yet accurate cell type annotation remains a significant challenge. Inconsistent labels, technological variability, and limitations in transferring annotations from reference datasets hinder precise annotation. This study presents a novel approach for accurate cell type annotation in scRNA-seq data using unique marker gene sets. By manually curating cell type names and markers from 280 publications, we verified marker expression profiles across these datasets and unified the nomenclature to consistently identify 166 cell types and subtypes. Our customized algorithm, which builds on the AUCell method, achieves accurate cell labeling at single-cell resolution and surpasses the performance of reference-based tools like Azimuth, especially in distinguishing closely related subtypes. To enhance accessibility and practical utility for researchers, we have also developed a user-friendly application that automates the cell typing process, enabling efficient verification and supporting comprehensive downstream analyses.

Single cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) technologies provide unprecedented resolution representing transcriptomics at the level of single cell. One of the biggest challenges in scRNA-seq data analysis is the cell type annotation, which is usually inferred by cell separation approaches. In-silico algorithms that accurately identify individual cell types in ongoing single-cell sequencing studies are crucial for unlocking cellular heterogeneity and understanding the biological basis of diseases. In this study, we focus on robustly identifying cell types in single-cell RNA sequencing data; we conduct a comparative analysis using methods established in biology, like Seurat, Leiden, and WGCNA, as well as Infomap, statistical inference via Stochastic Block Models (SBM), and single-cell Graph Neural Networks (scGNN). We also analyze preprocessing pipelines to identify and optimize key components in the process. Leveraging two independent datasets, PBMC and ROSMAP, we employ clustering algorithms on cell-cell networks derived from gene expression data. Our findings reveal that while clusters detected by WGCNA exhibit limited correspondence with cell types, those identified by multiresolution Infomap and Leiden, and SBM show a closer alignment, with Infomap standing out as a particularly effective approach. Infomap notably offers valuable insights for the precise characterization of cellular landscapes related to neurodegenration and immunology in scRNA-seq.

sample_q_texts: Native long-read sequencing provides critical insights into mammalian single-cell biology, yet its representation in single-cell models faces challenges. Current methods require sequences with predictable patterns in order to mimic the precision of high-throughput sequencing but lack the correct resolution. We introduce HiSeqAll -- an adapter-independent approach for representing natural human single-cell genomes in modern high-throughput sequencing models. In this project, we identify adapters with log2 ratios (L2) of 2.9 and 3.4 as potential candidates for representing mammalian long reads. We evaluated their performance as four different mapping criteria: VSM (Validity Score Matrix), Yijian Ranks, Max Encodings, and K-Means clustering. Finally, we demonstrated that our representation retains more genetic information than previously reported methods and outperforms them in all four criteria. We envision this platform will greatly assist in comparing cell properties across platforms, offering additional resolution and signal to noise ratio, particularly when sequencing epigenomes.

Genetic analysis of genetic variation in mice has revealed distinct genomic structures for highland and lowland populations. To study the role of genetic variation, population structure and gene-environment interaction, we used genomic genotyping data and identified 51 repetitive elements enriched in highland populations. For each polymorphism, the pathogenicity effects of the polymorphism was studied in 19 strains derived from two highland populations (Ulu and Monte Fuji) by using a stochastic Monte-Carlo-simulation model. The commonest polymorphism, which affected 15 repetitive elements, generated a QTL for disease resistance in Monte Fuji and the recessive allele in the upland population. We found polymorphism effects to be completely determined by genome structure. Polymorphism was common in common cis-elements but very rare in trans-elements. Polymorphism was enriched in isolated tandem repeats, but rare in euchromatic genomes. These findings provide insight into the structure of repetitive elements, the possible effects of genotype on disease resistance and the unique role of repetitive elements in genetic mapping.

Plenary common genes are predicted to be duplicated in more than 77\% of human diseases, yet the causal relevance of these genomic aberrations remains elusive. Here we assessed the relevance of structural and functional changes in common genes to a series of structural and functional alterations in 39 different disease-prone loci selected from the ClinVar database. We report that nine genes showed evidence of causal relevance, with the highest evidence coming from mutations in a candidate gene interacting with TLR5. These findings highlight the need for comparative analyses across models to address the function of structural variations in disease-prone loci.

TLDR - We report the relevance of microdeletions in TLR5 interacting region to a series of microdeletions in structural genes.

The influence of denaturing on sample preparation for high-resolution shotgun sequencing is well documented, but little is known about how sequence depth impacts analytical results in clinical samples. This is particularly challenging because fast-spinning sequencing platforms and low-avidity adapters are often applied to clinical samples, which result in rapid loss of sequence depth. Here, we developed an accurate and reproducible method to simulate multiple sequencing depths with clinical data. Using two healthy adults as model subjects, we assessed whether denaturing and resequencing induced batch effects with current sequencing methods. We then analyzed the sequence depth information for 30 clinical samples from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, chronic rhinitis, chronic urticaria, chronic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, chronic pericarditis, arthritis, osteoarthritis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, chronic skin diseases, and stomach ulcers. We demonstrated that, regardless of source, highly multiplexed (e.g., 15-plex) or unmultiplexed (e.g., 10-plex) data can faithfully simulate complete sequence depth on the same instrument, demonstrating the robustness of current sequencing platforms. Using clinically-available natural human DNA, we confirmed that sequencing depth preserved the natural complexity of RNA transcripts without detectable loss in complexity. Our results show that human samples, which are frequently used in clinical studies, are more suitable for clinical sample sequencing using current sequencing technologies. We anticipate that our approach will enable more precise and accurate analyses of clinical samples in future studies.

Population selection is the most widely used technique in DNA sequencing, but downstream analyses have been limited by difficulties in obtaining high quality read data. Sequence assembly, a common preprocessing step, often requires extensive manual processing. Because de novo assembly can yield a 'much' coverage profile for individual regions, this process requires identifying regions that will have relatively high coverage of the assembly, followed by assembly and quality control of the regions. While there are approaches to conducting this process manually, they are costly in time and data, as the manual process increases the likelihood of redundant assembly. To alleviate this, we developed an automatic approach that identifies regions of high and low coverage by comparing the average longest read lengths across different genomes, leading to a more informed de novo assembly strategy. We validated the approach on a simulated alignment of 40,000 proteins, identifying more than 10,000 orphan proteins that were later confirmed by manual identification. The resulting read alignment of these orphan proteins was then preprocessed to improve the quality of the read. For the de novo assembly, we ran the inter-genome gap generator GloBay 1.2 on these assembled regions. The assembly was assessed by comparing the quality of the resulting clusters with a formal metrics that is defined by the selection of sequence context. Using this algorithm, we identified regions in the GloBay assemblies that were enriched in read target positions. We applied this approach to 38 orphan proteins in human genomes that were subsequently validated by manual identification.

This study focuses on the likelihood of post-transcriptional preservation of first exons for microsatellite-associated genomic rearrangements. The primary aim is to assess the significance of the first exons, considering their loss during the genomic rearrangement process. Subsequently, the primary exons are associated with a novel identification method, which aims to analyse the complexity of the initial rearrangement process. Notably, this study contributes to the understanding of how individual exons influence overall genomic rearrangements. By applying different statistical models to the exon repertoire and whole genome sequences, the analysis focuses on the relationships between microhomology arms and exon composition, which often play a significant role in the occurrence of gene conversion in trans (GC-trans) of microsatellite associated genes. This approach offers a holistic insight into how genes and transcriptional units are integrated within the overall rearrangement process.

The Gencode assembly protocol, GAIT, generates assembly programs containing high-quality 100-3kb chromosome maps for many species, including humans. This procedure is based on four separate phases. The initial phase only needs a single GCF-annotated chromosome; subsequently, NTI and capsids need to be produced. Capsids, the first step, creates ten additional smaller files for each chromosome, one per species. These capsids are then processed into a single GFA-1 header file, which is used as the input to PHASE I. Finally, the resultant GCF program is run to extract the contigs and map the assemblies to the correct human chromosomes. After compiling chromosome maps in the GCF it is often the case that other fragments are also present on the chromosome (such as from genome-wide resequencing or exome capture), which are now likely present as polymorphisms. To determine whether these polymorphisms may have an effect on chromosome mobility, the GFA system was investigated for inclusion of these data. For this, we developed a pipeline using PHASE II+INFO+ tagset to identify genomes. This pipeline outputs an accurate and fast representation of genome context. Importantly, the contigs produced by GAIT may not be exhaustive, leading to missing genomic material. Using this approach, we implemented GFA in a custom pipeline that can be used to clean up contigs and add new data for the resulting GFA contigs. We demonstrate that these data can be added in a sensible way by validating the genome to sequence pairs previously identified as missing to GFA data. The GFA framework offers a way to extract, automate, and store sequence data from many sources, making the platform suitable for genomics to provide novel genomic data in a standardised manner to support research into ageing and inherited diseases.

Single-cell sequencing can be used to identify genomic regions associated with pathogenic conditions, but finding the genomic locations of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) can be a difficult task. Here we present KSHV-p53 (KSH5-family protein) binding sites within the exonic regions of two KSHV-mediated human cancers (orally transmitted HVC and cutaneous HVC), as well as three HVC reference genomes. We identified a land-marker for KSHV p53 binding, which we annotated and classified into three overlapping groups based on the sequence context: (i) variable amino acid residues, (ii) conserved dinucleotide repeat sequences, and (iii) two novel motifs (1). KSH5-binding sites were validated with anti-KSHV monoclonal antibodies, and further annotated based on published database annotations and sequence homology with KSHV-p53 binding sites. We also evaluated the significance of KSH5-binding sites by assessing their density in disease tissues and KSHV-mediated tumor genomes. Together, our findings identify land-markers for KSH5-binding proteins as well as putative binding sites for both KSHV and KSHV-mediated tumors, which we propose contribute to KSHV-mediated cancers.

We demonstrate that this prolonged S-phase can be influenced by multiple mechanisms, in particular those that disrupt the integrity of the chromosomal structure. A-hierarchy model for homologous chromosome 1 (chr1) and 3 (chr3) translocation is proposed, based on genome-wide position effects. It integrates different categories of data: (1) genome-wide position effect estimates (GE-PE), which predict the impact of variation on genomic distance; (2) an unbalanced set of haplotype data with different confidence levels (HDPs), each representing individuals with a variant allele at different frequencies; and (3) an expected number of reads per position. The model proposes that this effective mix of data better represents true evolutionary history. Then, it is possible to estimate the effect of each variant at a specific location in the chromosome, using GE-PE.

The model was successfully tested using simulated data. It also identified three types of haplotypes with low confidence for most consumers of variant data. For instance, index polymorphisms are prevalent in both unbalanced and HDP data sets. To assess model performance, we also evaluated the effect of different effects on consumers of both datasets. The model is able to distinguish haplotypes at different frequencies of occurrence with GE-PE (false-positive rate) or haplotype shares, thereby correctly identifying significant haplotypes from each of the two datasets (false-negative rate). Importantly, the model correctly predicted haplotype frequencies at each location (false-positive rate) or haplotype shares, respectively, for consumers of either dataset (false-negative and false-positive rate). Importantly, the model was able to account for the evolutionarily conflict between heterozygosity and stability in the genome (false-positive rate).

Additionally, the model was able to explain and distinguish the haplotypes at each stage of their evolutionary conflict (false-positive rate), and estimated their effects on consumers of both sets of haplotypes (false-negative and false-positive rates). Importantly, the model also explained and distinguished genotypes and haplotypes at each stage of their evolutionary conflict (false-positive rate), and estimated their effects on consumers of both sets of haplotypes (false-positive rate). Finally, the model predicted gene expression changes and impact of haplotypes on functional regions (false-positive rate).

We used a Bayesian framework and both genomic and clinical data to identify and validate a model of disease-related mutations from an adult-onset disease (osteonecrosis of the proximal femur). After initial lung, pelvis, and hip bone formation, most mutations disappear from skeletal tissue. Within these bones, mutations are more abundant in younger adults, males, and smokers, suggesting more variation in bone cells. We then studied aging bone marrow cells, which showed marked heterogeneity both in terms of rare variants, which were primarily T-cell and macrophage genes; and in gene composition. We found considerable differences in the number of rare mutations between bone marrow cells and skeletal tissue; and in their diversity as a function of age, sex, and atrophy. Finally, we used transcriptomics, RNA-sequencing, and deep learning approaches to identify genes that correlate with human osteonecrosis, hip fracture, and periosteum-related fractures in the hip.

A unifying framework for both clinical and genomic data for osteonecrosis.

sample_p_texts: Tandem repeats are a class of genetic variation characterized by repetitions of DNA motifs of diverse sequences and lengths. Pentameric motifs, in particular, do not align with the protein-coding reading frames, often confining them to the less extensively studied non-coding portion of the genome. Intronic pentanucleotide tandem repeats are associated with 11 neurological disorders. Their pathogenic genotypes are primarily characterized by large length expansion and, unlike most repeat expansion disorders, have required a deviation from the reference motif. The population-level variability of pentameric repeats remains poorly understood due to technical limitations of short-read sequencing technologies. To address this knowledge gap, we genotyped 28,446 pentanucleotide repeat loci in 1,027 long-read PacBio HiFi samples from self-identified Black and African American participants in the All of Us Research Program. We developed new algorithms for tandem repeat decomposition, characterization, and visualization to facilitate this analysis. Our findings reveal extensive genome-wide heterogeneity in repeat length and sequence composition. Alleles with DNA sequences containing segments of distinct motifs were observed in 15% of loci. Additionally, 8% of loci exhibited multimodal repeat length distributions, in which distinct sequence compositions were often associated with distinct length ranges. Repeat loci were highly enriched in proximity to transposable elements, including 68% mapping to Alu elements, a retrotransposon specific to primates. Comparative analysis of the reference sequences from 30 species, including 27 primates, suggests that most pentanucleotide repeats fully emerged in a common ancestor of humans and other ape species, or even within more closely related hominin lineages. As an example, we describe a highly polymorphic and recently evolved repeat locus in the ABCA1 gene, a major regulator of cellular cholesterol and phospholipid homeostasis. This study provides novel and comprehensive insights into the evolutionary formation of pentamer tandem repeat loci and their extensive variability across human genomes.

The ribosome is one of the core macromolecules in the cell. The ribosomal RNAs (rRNA), which are essential components of the ribosome, are coded by the multi-copy ribosomal DNA (rDNA). Despite its highly conserved function, the rDNA displays substantial variation within all species analysed to date. This variation comprises both inter-individual differences in total copy number (CN) as well as inter- and intragenomic sequence variation in the form of single nucleotide variants (SNV) and insertions/deletions (INDELs) across rDNA copies. Whether germline variation of rDNA sequence associates with phenotypic traits in humans is, to date, unknown. Here, using the UK Biobank whole genome sequencing data, we first derive a high confidence list of rDNA-associated SNVs and INDELs that we validate in multiple ways. Using this list, we show that specific rDNA variants associate with several human traits. In particular, traits associated with body size appear enriched in variants within the Expansion Segment 15L region in the 28S rRNA. The strength of these associations does not diminish when accounting for the total rDNA CN of each individual. Our work represents the first large-scale association analysis of human traits with germline sequence variation in the rDNA, a source of human complex trait-relevant genetic variation that has thus far been largely ignored.

In addition to the issues pointed out in Tabin et al1, the MZR data from Zhang et. al 20222 are suggestive of high levels of contamination from a source similar to modern Han Chinese, the majority population in the country where MZR was sequenced. In fact, MZR can be modeled entirely as Han-related ancestry and noise. These results raise further concerns about the veracity of the MZR data and thus the papers historical conclusions.

The importance of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) in numerous biological processes, including DNA synthesis and cellular energy production, underscores the need for therapeutic and public health strategies to address B12 insufficiency/deficiency in the population. Genetic variations in pathways influencing cobalamin absorption, transport, and metabolism can affect various direct and indirect measures of vitamin B12 status. To facilitate a structured approach to studying these genetic factors, we aimed to systematically curate and create a user-friendly web database that offers comprehensive data on genetic variants influencing B12 biomarkers. A Pubmed search was performed for 5 B12 traits (total serum/plasma B12, holotranscobalamin (active B12), total transcobalamin, holo haptocorrin, and methylmalonic acid) resulting in 493 research publications, of which 47 relevant publications were reviewed further. The database backend was built using MongoDB and the web interface was coded in PHP, JavaScript, HTML and CSS on an Apache HTTP server. We have manually curated and compiled the Cobalamin Associated Genetic Variant (CobVar) database, comprising a total of 324 genetic variant associations for 5 different vitamin B12 traits involving 222 unique genetic variants and 84 genes identified across several genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and candidate gene studies. About one-third of the total genetic variant associations have been reported in >1 independent studies and 15 variants in >1 ethnic group. FUT2 gene showed the maximum number of associations for total serum/plasma B12 (N=39), followed by MTHFR (N=24) and TCN2 (N=23). The database is accessible online at https://datatools.sjri.res.in/VBG/. CobVar is a vital resource for researchers and nutritionists, offering quick access to the latest developments in B12-related genetic variant research and serves as a valuable tool for advancing personalized treatment.

Non-canonical (non-B) DNA structures-bent DNA, slipped-strand structures, palindromes and hairpins, triplex DNA, G-quadruplexes, etc.-which form at certain sequence motifs (A-phased repeats, direct repeats, inverted repeats, mirror repeats, etc.), have recently emerged as important regulators of many cellular processes and as drivers of genome evolution. Yet, they have been understudied due to their highly repetitive nature and potentially inaccurate sequences when examined with short-read technologies. The recent availability of human and other ape telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genomes, which were generated with long reads, provides an opportunity to study the repertoire of non-canonical DNA motifs comprehensively. Here we characterized non-B DNA motifs in the T2T genomes of human and six non-human apes-bonobo, chimpanzee, gorilla, Bornean orangutan, Sumatran orangutan, and siamang. We found that non-B DNA motifs are enriched at the genomic regions that were added to these T2T assemblies as compared to previous assembly versions. Non-B DNA motifs occupied 9-15%, 9-11%, and 12-38% of autosomal, chromosome X, and chromosome Y sequences, respectively. Gorilla had the highest percentage of its genome occupied by non-B DNA motifs. The same DNA sequences were frequently annotated with multiple non-B DNA motif types. Several types of non-B DNA motifs had high densities at short arms of acrocentric chromosomes and non-canonical structures might contribute to satellite dynamics in these regions. Most centromeres showed an enrichment in at least one non-B DNA motif type, consistent with the role of non-B structures in determining centromeres. Our results highlight the uneven distribution of predicted non-B DNA structures across ape genomes and suggest their novel functions in the previously inaccessible genomic regions.

SummaryQuality control is a fundamental but often neglected step in any NGS pipeline. Detecting issues like cross-sample contamination and sample swaps is essential to control the data integrity. Here, we present NGSTroubleFinder, a novel python tool to detect cross-sample contamination in human Whole-Genome and Whole-Transcriptome Sequencing data, sample swaps and mismatches between the reported and the inferred genetic and transcriptomic sexes. NGSTroubleFinder is implemented in Python and incorporates a custom-built parallelized pileup engine written in C. The tool reports extensive information on the samples both in textual and HTML format including key plots for easy interpretation of the results.

Availability and ImplementationNGSTroubleFinder is written in Python and C, and it can be easily installed with pip. The tool source code and the models are freely available on github (https://github.com/STALICLA-RnD/NGSTroubleFinder) and a containerized version is available on dockerhub (https://hub.docker.com/r/staliclarnd/ngstroublefinder).

High throughput sequencing technologies have become essential in the fields of evolutionary biology and genomics. When dealing with non-model organisms or genomic gigantism, sequencing whole genomes is still relatively costly and therefore reduced-genome representations are frequently obtained, for instance by  target capture approaches. While computational tools exist that can handle target capture data and identify small-scale variants such as single nucleotide polymorphisms and micro-indels, options to identify large scale structural variants are limited. To meet this need, we introduce PAV-spotter: a tool that can identify presence/absence variation (PAV) in target capture data. PAV-spotter conducts a signal cross-correlation calculation, in which the distribution of read counts per target between samples of different a priori defined classes - e.g. male versus female, or diseased versus healthy - are compared. We apply and test our methodology by studying Triturus newts: salamanders with gigantic genomes that currently lack an annotated reference genome. Triturus newts suffer from a hereditary disease that kills half their offspring during embryogenesis. We compare the target capture data of two different types of diseased embryos, characterized by unique deletions, with those of healthy embryos. Our findings show that PAV-spotter helps to expose such structural variants, even in the face of medium to low sequencing coverage levels, low sample sizes, and background noise due to mis-mapped reads. PAV-spotter can be used to study the structural variation underlying supergene systems in the absence of whole genome assemblies. The code, including further explanation on how to use and customize it, is available through the PAV-spotter GitHub repository: https://github.com/Wielstra-Lab/PAVspotter.

Copy number variants (CNVs) are prevalent in both diploid and haploid genomes, with the latter containing a single copy of each gene. Studying CNVs in genomes from single or few cells is significantly advancing our knowledge in human disorders and disease susceptibility. Low-input including low-cell and single-cell sequencing data for haploid and diploid organisms generally displays shallow and highly non-uniform read counts resulting from the whole genome amplification steps that introduce amplification biases. In addition, haploid organisms typically possess relatively short genomes and require a higher degree of DNA amplification compared to diploid organisms. However, most CNV detection methods are specifically developed for diploid genomes without specific consideration of effects on haploid genomes. Challenges also reside in reference samples or normal controls which are used to provide baseline signals for defining copy number losses or gains. In traditional methods, references are usually pre-specified from cells that are assumed to be normal or disease-free. However, the use of pre-defined reference cells can bias results if common CNVs are present. Here, we present the development of a comprehensive statistical framework for data normalization and CNV detection in haploid single- or low-cell DNA sequencing data called HapCNV. The prominent advancement is the construction of a novel genomic location specific pseudo-reference that selects unbiased references using a preliminary cell clustering method. This approach effectively preserves common CNVs. Using simulations, we demonstrated that HapCNV outperformed existing methods by generating more accurate CNV detection, especially for short CNVs. Superior performance of HapCNV was also validated in detecting known CNVs in a real P. falciparum parasite dataset. In conclusion, HapCNV provides a novel and useful approach for CNV detection in haploid low-input sequencing datasets, with easy applicability to diploids.

sample_q_texts: Elucidating the dynamics of transcriptomes in complex regulatory systems is challenging and relies on efficient computational and statistical approaches. Here, we develop and explore novel predictors based on machine learning techniques, which we call dynamic regulator (DR) models, designed to capture, monitor, and control long-term gene expression changes in the context of specific regulatory networks. These models are robust, capable of differentiating between various regulatory interactions and maintaining the flexibility to accommodate changes in the system. We demonstrate their performance and interpret the performance-predictability trade-off of our models in various scenarios, showing that computational, and statistical predictions are highly correlated, with a typical wide area and depth accuracy-robustness trade-off across diverse application domains. We additionally present an integrated framework that enables the combination of long-term predictions with current knowledge of gene regulatory networks, enhancing the efficacy of the proposed models for real-world problems. Our work paves the way for leveraging dynamic regulator models as effective tools for dynamically adapting gene regulatory networks in diverse application domains, offering a paradigm shift in regulatory control strategies, enabling context-aware and adaptive control in various fields such as disease modeling, computational biology, and artificial intelligence, enhancing the adaptability and robustness of systems in response to changes.

Large-scale multi-omics datasets have captured the spatial distributions of environmental gradients for only a limited amount of time, often resulting in incomplete information. Such landscapes can be characterized using Cellular-Based Conservation Laws (CBCLs) to predict functions in conserved genomes and estimate relationships between markers for the functions. Yet, for landscape modeling purposes, we expect that functions are derived from gene regulatory interactions. In our study, we assess the impact of missing the cascade of molecular interactions in the function from the non-uniform distribution of the continuous function across genome space. We demonstrate this by using different functions to predict functions of systems with missing regulatory interactions from conserved regions in the genome. We show that functions performed relatively worse for functions of genome regions derived only from a conserved regulatory regulatory model, which include regulatory motifs, regulatory components, promoters, non-coding promoters, or an allosteric component, suggesting that functional relationships modeled may be incomplete. This functional deficiency, however, is not due to interactions, but to the use of the underlying functional model. We identify that regulatory models derived from gene regulatory interaction design can address the same function deficiency as functions derived from classical modeling approaches. The present study shows that such incompleteness does not compromise the function. Our findings have implications for landscape modeling, suggesting that functional models are best generated from direct relationships between space- and time-dependent metrics of genomic interactions. Further, this framework may serve as a powerful tool for understanding the functional relationships in a broader perspective.

Single-cell transcriptomics provides an unprecedented view of cellular functions, but current genomic-scale models struggle to accurately interpret expression and function of complex networks in cells. Here, we introduce CellularGravity, a Bayesian framework that learns to map the ensemble of transcriptional measurements from cells across time into state representations in genotype space using a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN-D). Consistent with prior time-series modeling approaches, we establish (i) a generalizable, probabilistic framework that can (ii) model the relative state dynamics of independent subsets of cells across multiple time windows and (iii) distinguish different dynamical states of cells. Our empirical findings for our canonical single-cell transcriptional datasets from Epics and Ensembl are in broad agreement with our results for supervised single-cell transcriptomics using binary classifiers. For instance, we find that our framework can capture and accurately predict the dynamical state of cells over a wide range of temporal dynamics, even in cases where the number of measurements is small. Moreover, we apply our framework to explore genomic long-term evolution (GGEV-D), a fundamental paradigm of transcriptional dynamics in cells in response to varying environmental changes. By using a single-cell measure of evolution, CellularGravity can enable inference of dynamical state transitions within genes and networks.

Cell fate decision making in eukaryotic cells is governed by a complex interaction between network-level dynamics, regulated by topology, limited-time scales and selection pressure, and local processes, minimally impacted by wider dynamics. However, the dynamics of individual cells are only observable for relatively short periods of time and it is unclear whether the temporal hierarchy of cell fate decisions is preserved at the cell-level. To address this, we monitored transient signalling cascades in single differentiated cells within S. cerevisiae, and used single molecule imaging to track single molecules over tens of hours. We provide experimental evidence that the temporal hierarchy of gene activation can persist and maintain a positive feedback effect across individual cells, even when cell-level activity can no longer be observed for longer than a few days. Our results suggest that the memory effect of cell-specific gene activations enables cell-level maintenance of signalling regulation with an observed shift towards transient signalling processes over time. Finally, we highlight how our approach, especially single-molecule tracking, can uncover spatial activity patterns at subcellular resolution.

Importantly, the authors showed that the inclusion of information about when a gene was activated during transcription (termed 'average mutational load' - AM) could significantly alter transcription time predictions. Yet, the potential value of AM as a latent variable in transcriptomics research, without the need for temporally relevant information, has remained largely unexplored. We show that AM is an effective latent variable for local and global transcriptomic analyses. We identified the AM-based features at single-cell levels, which accurately captured important functional relationships between genes from the averaged signals from cross-species experiments. Moreover, AM-based approaches provided accurate, unbiased estimates of time-averaged activation profiles for expression data from the same cross-species experiments. Our findings demonstrate that AM is a sensitive, and therefore computationally tractable, biomarker of transcription in single-cell studies. The current findings suggest that AM could be a useful biomarker of biological processes such as tissue homeostasis. These findings establish a method for latent variable marker identification from single-cell microarray data.

The temporal dynamics of cellular gene expression upon exposure to chemical perturbations in multicellular organisms remains poorly understood. Visualizing gene expression trajectories in real time can reveal critical cellular processes such as phase transitions and periods of quiescence, enabling the discovery of novel regulatory signals and mechanisms. Here, we describe a method for real-time monitoring of transcription factor activity and chromatin accessibility by stable cell lines transiently transfected with fluorescently tagged transcription factors. We used this method to identify increased noise in transcription factor expression upon prolonged exposure to a diverse set of bioactive agents, with robust detection of signal-dependent changes in chromatin accessibility in liver and blood liver micropump lung progenitors. Real-time transcriptional profiling also detected robust transcriptional changes in glial and hematopoietic cells exposed to a wide range of beta-carbenic acid in blood, but not in liver. This work demonstrates the utility of real-time transcriptional profiling to identify temporal dynamics of gene expression upon exposure to chemical perturbations.

How cells and tissues adapt to changing environments remains poorly understood. Current genetics-based studies of tissue responses provide models for such studies; however, they do not capture the full complexity of temporal phenomena of interest, including: cellular processes that enable migration, differentiation and tissue formation; diverse fates that can be altered by proliferation or post-mitotic fate decisions; and changes in molecular and cellular state such as inflammation and death that accompany disease progression or regeneration. Here we combine work in Computational Systems Biology with advances in in silico modeling to develop a machine-learning framework for modeling, interpreting, and optimizing interactions of genes and environmental factors. Specifically, we developed a deep convolutional neural network model for learning functional relationships between genes and environmental factors, and developed an event-based approach to predict the effect of different environments on cells.

Our work has revealed the full dynamics of tissue response in model systems. By modeling relationships between genes and environmental factors, we identified key regulators of tissue responses that were previously overlooked; by integrating model results with laboratory and clinical data, we learned how these regulators coordinate tissue responses to injury, inflammation, and regeneration. This framework offers new perspectives on tissue responses, and new ways to predict cellular responses to changing conditions.

Genetic expression changes during time cause biological and metabolic changes. In a previous work, we proposed a scenario where genetic perturbations during time are expressed as differential networks dynamics. We aim to build a data-driven methodology that identifies genes with the changes during time and based on those genes can predict networks dynamics. We selected the differential activation probability (DAP) and the differential expression probability (DEP) to measure the dynamics. First, we applied our method to a small set of genes and implemented it using a Python package. Next, we developed and evaluated an algorithm to identify genes based on a set of specific keywords. Our approach relies on the Pearson correlation coefficient to infer the impact of the identified genes. We also applied it to a set of fluorescent probes. To evaluate the robustness of our model, we conducted a simulation study with a set of published genes. Finally, we applied our method to a set of metabolic reactions, and we also generated a set of control genes. Our results show that, in general, the identification of genes based on the Pearson correlation coefficient, improves the performance.

In order to extract the true underlying biological signals from the enormous amount of time series data generated in many research fields, signal separation has become an essential preprocessing step. Traditional approaches to signal separation rely heavily on statistical models, but do not consider the relationships between functional genes in the biological system. We developed a new hierarchical (e.g., signal | conditioning genes) and flexible (e.g., weak signs of interest | weak signs of local maxima) model-free clustering algorithm to simultaneously separate the functional genes. The strong separation and sensitivity to local fluctuations of the weak signs of interest are achieved by clustering the functional genes in the hierarchical (e.g., Poisson regression) hierarchical model, which is followed by thresholding the local maxima of the conditional posterior to obtain the final signal | conditioning genes. The hierarchical weak signs of interest are further conditioned on the local fluctuations of the functional genes. The proposed model-free clustering technique combined both signal separation and local fluctuation analysis to obtain the final signal | conditioning genes for experimental data. We validated the performance of the proposed hierarchical signal separation method using a genome-scale RNA-seq dataset with 32,153 zebrafish transcriptomes in a fold change of 2.45. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method could separate the functional genes with high sensitivity and confidence for both normal and pathological situations, and further showed that the performance of the method is stable for different experimental conditions.
sample_p_texts: The complex transcriptional regulatory relationships among genes influence gene expression levels and play crucial roles in determining cellular phenotypes. Here, we present a novel distributed large-scale transcriptional regulatory neural network model (DLTRNM) by integrating prior knowledge into the reconstruction of pre-trained machine learning models followed with fine-tuning. Taken S. cerevisiae as the example, the transcriptional regulatory relationships, carefully compiled and documented, are utilized to define interactions between TFs and their TGs within DLTRNM. Subsequently, DLTRNM is pre-trained on pan-transcriptomic data and fine-tuned with time-series data, enabling it to accurately predict dynamic regulatory correlations between TFs and TGs, such as simulating TG responses by tuning the expression of TFs. In addition, DLTRNM can assist in identifying potential key TFs for a subset of genes, thus simplifying the complex and interrelated transcriptional regulatory networks (TRN). Based on the key TFs, it can also refine previously reported transcriptional regulatory subnetworks and highlight the core regulatory networks. DLTRNM offers a powerful tool for studying transcriptional regulation with reduced computational demands and enhanced interpretability. Thus, this study represents a significant step forward in systems biology for understanding the complicated transcriptional regulation within cells.

Molecular signaling networks drive a diverse range of cellular decisions, including whether to proliferate, how and when to die, and many processes in between. Such networks often connect hundreds of proteins, genes, and processes. Understanding these complex networks is aided by computational modeling, but these tools require extensive programming knowledge. In this article, we describe a user-friendly, programming-free network simulation tool called Netflux (https://github.com/saucermanlab/Netflux). Over the last decade, Netflux has been used to construct numerous predictive network models that have deepened our understanding of how complex biological networks make cell decisions. Here, we provide a Netflux tutorial that covers how to construct a network model and then simulate network responses to perturbations. Upon completion of this tutorial, you will be able to construct your own model in Netflux and simulate how perturbations to proteins and genes propagate through signaling and gene-regulatory networks.

Time-series studies are critical for uncovering dynamic biological processes, but achieving comprehensive profiling and resolution across multiple time points and modalities (multi-omics) remains challenging due to cost and scalability constraints. Current methods for studying temporal dynamics, whether at the bulk or single-cell level, often require extensive sampling, making it impractical to deeply profile all time points and modalities. To overcome these limitations, we present DTPSP, a deep learning framework designed to identify the most informative time points in any time-series study, enabling resource-efficient and targeted analyses. DTPSP models temporal gene expression patterns using readily obtainable data, such as bulk RNA-seq, to select time points that capture key system dynamics. It also integrates a deep generative module to infer data for non-sampled time points based on the selected time points, reconstructing the full temporal trajectory. This dual capability enables DTPSP to prioritize key time points for in-depth profiling, such as single-cell sequencing or multi-omics analyses, while filling gaps in the temporal landscape with high fidelity. We apply DTPSP to developmental and disease-associated time courses, demonstrating its ability to optimize experimental designs across bulk and single-cell studies. By reducing costs, enabling strategic multi-omics profiling, and enhancing biological insights, DTPSP provides a scalable and generalized solution for investigating dynamic systems.

Gene expression is the primary modality being studied to differentiate between biological cells. Contemporary single-cell studies simultaneously measure genome-wide transcription levels for thousands of individual cells in a single experiment. While the characterization of cell population differences has often occurred through differential expression analysis, tiny effect sizes become statistically significant when thousands of cells are available for each population, compromising biological interpretation. Moreover, these large studies have spurred the development of methods to infer gene regulatory networks (GRNs) directly from the data, and GRN databases are becoming more comprehensive.

In this work, we propose a statistical model for gene expression measures and an inference method that leverage GRNs to deconvolve transcription factor (TF) activity from gene expression, by probabilistically assigning mRNA molecules to TFs. This shifts the paradigm from investigating gene expression differences to regulatory differences at the level of TF activity, aiding interpretation and allowing prioritization of a limited number of TFs responsible for significant contributions to the observed gene expression differences. The inferred TF activities result in intuitive prioritization of TFs in terms of the (difference in) estimated number of molecules they produce, in contrast to other widely-used methods relying on arbitrary enrichment scores. Our model allows the incorporation of prior information on the regulatory potential between each TF and target gene through prior distributions, and is able to deal with both repressing and activating interactions. We compare our approach to other TF activity estimation methods using two simulation experiments and two case studies.

From bacteria to humans, most organisms showcase inherent 24-hour circadian rhythms, best exemplified by the sleep-wake cycle. These rhythms are remarkably widespread, governing hormonal, metabolic, physiological, and behavioral oscillations, and are driven by molecular clocks that orchestrate the rhythmic expression of thousands of genes throughout the body. Here, we generate single-cell RNA and ATAC multiomic data to simultaneously characterize gene expression and chromatin accessibility of [~]33,000 mouse liver cells across the 24-hour day. Our study yields several key insights, including: (i) detecting circadian rhythmicity in both discretized liver cell types and transient sub-lobule cell states, capturing space-time RNA and ATAC profiles in a cell-type- and cell-state-specific manner; (ii) delving beyond mean cyclic patterns to characterize distributions, accounting for gene expression stochasticity due to transcriptional bursting; (iii) interrogating multimodal circadian rhythmicity, encompassing RNAs, DNA regulatory elements, and transcription factors (TFs), while examining priming and lagging effects across modalities; and (iv) inferring spatiotemporal gene regulatory networks involving target genes, TFs, and cis-regulatory elements that controls circadian rhythmicity and liver physiology. Our findings apply to existing single-cell data of mouse and Drosophila brains and are further validated by time-series single molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization, as well as vast amounts of existing and orthogonal high-throughput data from chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing, capture Hi-C, and TF knockout experiments. Altogether, our study constructs a comprehensive map of the time-series transcriptomic and epigenomic landscapes that elucidate the function and mechanism of the liver peripheral clocks.

Transient surges in gene or protein expression often mark the key regulatory checkpoints that propel cells from one functional state to the next, yet they are easy to miss in sparse, noisy single-cell omics data. We introduce scTransient, a trajectory-inference pipeline integrated into our cloud-based single-cell analysis platform PSCS. scTransient transforms single-cell expression profiles into continuous pseudotime signals and couples them with wavelet-based signal processing to isolate short-lived but biologically meaningful bursts of activity. After ordering cells with unsupervised graph trajectories or supervised psupertime, scTransient windows expression values along pseudotime, applies a continuous wavelet transform, and assigns every gene a Transient-Event Score (TES) that rewards sharp, isolated coefficients while penalizing background fluctuations. Synthetic benchmarks show TES robustly recovers transient events across a wide range of cell numbers, signal-to-noise ratios, and event widths. Applying scTransient to three public datasets-- hematopoietic differentiation, monocyte-to-macrophage maturation, and single-cell proteomic cell-cycle progression--uncovers previously unreported, process-specific expression spikes. These include erythropoiesis regulators (e.g., Nfe2), membrane-raft remodeling proteins during macrophage differentiation, and S-phase DNA-replication factors in A549 cells. Functional enrichment confirms that top-scoring genes cluster into pathways directly pertinent to each transition. By extending trajectory inference from descriptive ordering to quantitative detection of fleeting regulatory programs, scTransient--now readily accessible via the PSCS web interface--offers researchers a practical route to uncovering transient molecular events that drive development, differentiation, and disease.
